first_run.title: The Web Summit team, part two: seven people, each with their own agent, a designer with little time, and every voice memo turned into a follow-up within the hour

A portfolio with a film first: Silvio Switha's site, made in under an hour by the site factory and five design agents, with his music video in the first screen, his agents as a solar system and a mixing desk, a producer's studio, a proposal for clients and a gig poster, and every claim something he built

A website that is her: how Yiheng Wang's site was made in three passes in one evening, by the site factory, five design agents and then her own agent, with five designs, a kitchen brigade of 26 agents, a printable brief and a page for your AI, and why every claim on it is something she can talk about because she did it

Specialist agents for every team: long-lived agents that keep one skill, design, UX, code, security, behaviour policies or writing, with a person who owns it, so that new teams start from our best work instead of from scratch, and why that makes expertise that never scaled into something you can hire, even from another company

The pitch: a site that looks better, that you own, that nobody can lock you into, that has almost nothing to attack, that costs once instead of every month, and that you change by talking to Claude, six promises, the proof behind each, and three designs for a site built on nothing else, "six promises", "just say it" and "stop renting your website"

Designing sovereignwebsite.ai: the brief for the team that will build the site of our first mass-market product, how the stack now has four layers, SGit, RiskMandate, AgentiCCells and Sovereign Website, six ways to say what it is, the ten pages, the sovereignty maturity model at its centre, how to build the site as a sovereign website itself, and five homepage designs to choose from

The sovereign website: a pivot brief for agenticcells.ai, what the site says today and what it should say next, sovereignty as the headline, a website you own, control, change and can run anywhere, the deliverables explained, the infographics to draw, five homepage designs to choose from, and the partner programme and examples that already prove it

One researcher for every newsroom: a research site that works as a light, focused Internet Archive for the sources our stories rest on, captured on a schedule into a pack a day, published by licence tier, and shared by the PHP site, the wires and the Web Summit newsroom

The Web Summit team, part five: the last day of setup, 180 releases, every person getting a key, an accountant counting the team's tokens, synthetic users testing the merch, and an inbox only the agents can write to

A website with a team inside: why a Sovereign Agentic Website is delivered not as a site but as a site with six or seven agents already set up and coordinated in its repository, a conductor, a designer, a writer, a developer, a reviewer, a translator and a keeper, each with a role and a behaviour policy, and what that means for the person who owns it
The value of constraints: what client-side encryption and open source actually gave us, which is not what you would think
A newsroom for one: the reading list I send by email became the first page of this newsroom for the people I write to, so it now says what it is, shows what they have read, and asks for an answer

Every story has an address: a design proposal for PrompTugal.news as a ground-up newsroom, where news is filed where it happens and climbs to the region and the country with its proof, mocked up from the live data of 19 local editions
sgit in a CI pipeline: encrypted, versioned data in and out of GitHub Actions, between its jobs, through write-only lanes, and a key for every job
Agentics, ready to sell: what we showed at Agentic Engineering Live, who else is selling agentic services and at what price, the engagement path, and a marketplace for the consultants who deliver it
The augmented book: one source in layers, projected to the web, the iPad and print, so the reader gets the right information at the right time, and what fifty years of attempts teach
A key for every person: how each person's conductor issues them a key for the team's site, seals what is for them, and how a signed message turns the public web into a channel the agents can trust

An inbox only your agents can write to: a conductor publishes one append lane per agent, each lane's token sealed to that agent's own key, so everything needed to talk privately is public and only the right agent can use it
Selling at the right altitude: why a small security firm's grand website is read by the people who will never buy from it, is unreadable to the ones who need it, and what to put on the page instead

A hub for agentic sites: every site AgentiCCells builds in a repository and an sgit vault, served at its own address, and listed on hub.agenticcells.site, where it can be found, promoted and copied as a template; with an orange grower as the first example

Atomic cells, end to end: the £500 website as AgentiCCells' first offering, an order on a queue, an agentic team that builds a public site, a customer who steers it from their browser with a key, and a handover, with no daily work for the founder

From a commit to a live website: a site factory where a request file in a commit makes a CI pipeline create the GitHub repository, the DNS record and the sgit vault, seed a page, check HTTPS, run a first pass with Claude Code, and record it all, so an agent can create sites by committing

CI behaviour policies: to create one repository and one DNS record per request, our site factory's pipeline holds the power to create, change or delete every repository in the organisation and to point any subdomain anywhere, and why pipelines now need the same behaviour policies as agents

Fork it: making forking the way people adopt our cells and template sites, as GitHub made it the way people adopt code, with five ways to make a cell yours, what a fork-ready repository needs, paths from one repository to the next, a hub that lets usage decide what we build, and the brief for the team

The cell is the unit: positioning AgentiCCells around small, focused cells, each with an objective, a deliverable and a behaviour policy, each with a page that sells it, a free recipe and three ways to get help, a catalogue that grows one need at a time, in each industry's own words, and why we should run our own work in cells first
